Employing micro-aeration in anaerobic digestion of poultry litter and 
wheat straw: Batch kinetics and continuous performance 
Yuanhang Zhan a,*, Jun Zhu a, Yiting Xiao a, Leland C. Schrader a, Sarah Xiao Wu b, 
Ndeddy Aka Robinson Jr b, Zhiwu Wang c 
a Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR 72701, USA

G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T

A B S T R A C T   
In this study, different micro-aeration (MA) strategies for anaerobic digestion (AD) of poultry litter (PL) and 
wheat straw (WS) were examined. MA at different stages (pretreatment, middle, pretreatment plus middle, and 
daily) in batch AD of WS showed that daily MA had the highest increase (16.5 %) of the cumulative methane 
yield (CMY) compared to the control. Batch co-digestion (Co-AD) of WS and PL with daily MA obtained a fur­
therly improved (15.1 %) CMY of 225.44 N mL CH4/g vS added. The modified Gompertz model and Cone model 
were good in fitting the methane yield kinetics of MA engaged AD process (R2 greater than 0.99). Daily MA 
shortened the lag phase of Co-AD by 3.4 %. The sequencing batch reactor for the Co-AD of WS and PL showed an 
increased (21.5 %) daily methane yield when 0.5-h/d MA was employed. The results provided support for the 
application of micro-aeration in the AD of agricultural wastes.   
1. Introduction 
Although anaerobic digestion (AD) has been widely applied to 
remediating agricultural wastes for producing methane containing 
biogas as a renewable energy resource, as reviewed by previous workers 
(Chen et al., 2008; Karki et al., 2021), the common AD process has

several drawbacks such as low hydrolysis rate, unstable at high organic 
loading rate (OLR), and release of toxic/corrosive hydrogen sulfide. 
However, it has been reported recently that all these problems could be 
overcome through applying micro-aeration to the AD process as previ­
ously reviewed by Nguyen and Khanal (2018). Micro-aeration was 
defined as an advanced technology by dosing small quantities of air or 
oxygen into the AD reactor to enhance the process efficiency (Botheju 
et al., 2010). The air or oxygen might be dosed either one time by in­
jection, intermittently (pulse-mode), or continuously, and the air or 
oxygen dosing might be conducted at different stages of the AD process 
(pretreatment, during digestion, or post digestion) (Girotto et al., 2018). 
Many researchers reported that with a small amount of energy input, 
micro-aeration showed great promise for improving AD process per­
formance in organic degradation and methane production (Lim & Wang, 
2013; D. Nguyen et al., 2019a; Xu et al., 2021). Zhen et al. (2021) 
applied micro-aeration pretreatment to the thermophilic (55 degrees 
Celsius (◦C)) anaerobic digestion of corn stalk in a batch reactor (0.5 L) 
and found that micro-aeration promoted the generation of volatile fatty 
acids (VFA), and the digesters with a micro-aeration rate of 1 mL O2/g 
volatile solids (VS) increased cumulative methane production by 13.2 
%. While Fu et al. (2015) conducted oxygen injection to a batch AD (37 
℃) of corn straw after experiencing an obvious decrease in methane 
yield and observed an increase in the yield by 28.5 % and an improve­
ment in the volatile solids (VS) removal efficiency by 29.4 %. Moreover, 
Fu et al. (2016) conducted another study on batch thermophilic AD of 
corn straw with daily micro-aeration and reported that the group with 
air injection rate of 12.5 mL/LR per day improved the methane yield 
(16.5 %) and the vS removal efficiency. However, no direct comparisons 
between these micro-aeration strategies in terms of improving methane 
yield have been made. In addition, the substrate used for micro-aeration 
assisted AD process was mostly single substrate including primary 
sludge, wastewater, food waste or straw. There was a lack of research on 
the application of micro-aeration for anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of 
agricultural waste, neither in batch nor in continuous flow operation 
mode. Thus, the effect of micro-aeration on methane yield efficiency and 
reaction kinetics of batch AD of agricultural wastes needs to be inves­
tigated. Also, the application of micro-aeration in continuous-flow AD of 
agricultural wastes is worth research as well. 
In this study, the batch mono-digestion (Mo-AD) of wheat straw (WS) 
with different micro-aeration strategies were first examined and 
compared to select the best strategy with the highest methane yield. 
Then, the batch Co-AD of WS and poultry litter (PL) was conducted to 
furtherly improve the methane yield efficiency. Kinetics analysis of both 
Mo-AD and Co-AD was performed based on the batch experiments to 
mechanically analyze the effects of micro-aeration on methane yield 
performance. Lastly, the performance of the sequencing batch reactor 
for the continuous Co-AD of WS and PL with micro-aeration was also 
examined. Based on the results, this study aimed to support for the 
application of micro-aeration for enhancing methane production effi­
ciency from AD of agricultural wastes. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Substrate and inoculum sludge 
2.1.1. Wheat straw and poultry litter 
The substrate used in this study for both anaerobic mono-digestion 
(Mo-AD) and co-digestion (Co-AD) experiments was wheat straw (WS) 
collected from the University of Arkansas grass farm (Fayetteville, USA). 
The raw straw was then stored in a 4  degreesC walk-in refrigerator prior 
to pretreatment if not used immediately. Poultry litter (PL) was used as a 
nitrogen source to be co-digested with straw in the Co-AD process. The 
raw poultry litter used in this study was collected from the bedding 
waste in a chicken house in a poultry farm (University of Arkansas - 
Applied Broiler Research Farm, AR, US) and was then stored in a 4 ℃ 
walk-in refrigerator prior to pretreatment if not used immediately. The 
collected raw WS and PL was first mechanically cut using a mill (Food 
Processor, Hamilton Beach, Inc. VA, USA) before being screened using a 
0.85 mm sieve (20 mesh) as suggested by Zahan et al. (2018b). The 
properties of the prepared WS and PL were summarized in Table 1. 
2.1.2. Inoculum 
The inoculum used for both the Mo-AD and the Co-AD was collected 
from a running anaerobic digester for methane fermentation and sieved 
through a 1.40 mm mesh to remove any large particles, after which it 
was then pre-incubated for seven days at 37 ℃ to remove any remaining 
biodegradable fraction of the sludge. The properties of the inoculum 
sludge were also shown in Table 1. 
2.2. Micro-aeration 
Different micro-aeration strategies were applied to the Mo-AD, 
including pretreatment micro-aeration (pMA, micro-aeration was 
employed in the initial stage); secondary micro-aeration (sMA, micro- 
aeration was employed in the middle stage at day 19 and day 20); 
pretreatment micro-aeration plus secondary micro-aeration (pMA +
sMA); and daily micro-aeration (dMA, micro-aeration was employed 
daily). Five identical batch reactors were used for the Mo-AD of WS with 
different micro-aeration strategies employed, i.e., the control group (C, 
no micro-aeration employed), pMA, sMA, pMA + sMA, and dMA. The 
specific micro-aeration date and micro-aeration rate of different micro- 
aeration strategies were adopted from suggestions made by previous 
workers (Fu et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2015; Lim & Wang, 2013) and detailed 
in Table 2. The corresponding volume of air was injected into the batch 
reactors using a syringe. In the Co-AD experiments, the same daily 
micro-aeration was employed as in the Mo-AD. 
2.3. Batch anaerobic digestion 
2.3.1. Anaerobic mono-digestion of wheat straw 
Five identical glass containers were used for Mo-AD of WS with 
different micro-aeration strategies employed. The glass container had a 
total volume of 648 mL, equipped with a gas outlet for biogas collection 
in Tedlar® gas bags (Tedlar Bag, CEL Scientific Corp., Cerritos, CA, 
USA). The glass container also had a tube reaching the sludge at the 
bottom of the reactor for nitrogen gas flushing and micro-aeration (air 
injection) as shown in Fig. 1 (a). To begin, 9.00 g of the wheat straw and 
200 mL of the inoculum sludge were placed into the reactor to reach a 
ratio of TSinoculum/TSsubstrate of 0.5 (Lim & Wang, 2013). Tap water was 
then added to the reactor to obtain a total working volume of 500 mL 
with pH adjusted to 8.00 with 1 N hydrochloric acid (HCl) solution and 
1 N sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution. Then, the reactor was purged 
with nitrogen gas for 5 min to eliminate oxygen before the reactor was 
fully sealed. After that, the Mo-AD batch reactors were operated with the 
corresponding micro-aeration strategies applied. The Tedlar® gas bags 
with biogas collected were replaced daily. The volume of the collected 
biogas was measured, and the biogas samples were analyzed for nitro­
gen gas (N2), methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), etc. Pretrial ex­
periments showed that the differences in the methane production

2.3.2. Anaerobic co-digestion of wheat straw and poultry litter 
Two identical glass containers with the same configuration as 
described above were used for Co-AD of WS and PL. For each reactor, the 
equivalent prepared WS and PL, 4.60 g each, were mixed and used as the 
substrate with 200 mL of the inoculum sludge added to reach the same 
ratio of TSinoculum/TSsubstrate of 0.5 as in the Mo-AD experiments. The 
two batch reactors were operated as the control (Co-C) and the Co-AD 
with micro-aeration (Co-MA). The daily micro-aeration scheme was 
employed in the Co-AD experiments based on the results of the Mo-AD 
experiments. The operational protocol of the Co-AD experiments was 
the same as that of Mo-AD experiments as described above in Section 
2.3.1. 
2.3.3. Kinetic analysis 
To examine the effect of micro-aeration on the kinetic parameters of 
AD process, five kinetic models: the first-order model; the modified 
Gompertz model; the Cone model, the transfer model; and the Chen and 
Hashimoto model were used to fit the methane yield from both the Mo- 
AD and Co-AD batch experiments in this study. The first-order kinetic 
model (Eq. (1)) was first described by Llabr´es-Luengo and Mata-Alvarez 
(1987), who assumed that hydrolysis was the rate-limiting step that 
governed the overall process (Li et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019). 
However, the first-order model could not predict the conditions for 
maximum methane yield or lag phase (Kafle & Chen, 2016). The 
modified Gompertz model (Eq. (2)) was first used to predict methane 
production rate in a batch digester corresponding to the specific growth 
rate of methanogenic bacteria (Lay et al., 1998), and later became a 
widely used empirical regression model that described cell density in 
terms of exponential growth rates and lag phase duration, which could 
be used to identify the maximum methane production potential and lag 
phase (Kafle & Chen, 2016). Besides, recent research has reported that 
the Cone model (Eq. (3)), which is an empiric model that can estimate 
the methane yield rate and the maximum cumulative methane yield, is 
better than the other models in fitting the performance data in methane 
production from co-digestion (El-Mashad, 2013; Zahan et al., 2018b). 
Some recent studies also used the Transfer model (Eq. (4)) and Chen and 
Hashimoto model (Eq. (5)) to fit the methane production data from 
anaerobic co-digestion process (Karki et al., 2022).

2.4. Continuous co-digestion in anaerobic sequencing batch reactor 
Two identical cylindrical anaerobic sequencing batch reactors 
(ASBR) (Fig. 1 (b)) were used for the Co-AD of PL and WS in a continuous 
mode. The total volume of each reactor was 18 L with a full working 
volume of 16 L and 2 L headspace for maintaining enough biogas partial 
pressure. Detailed design of the ASBR could be found in a previously 
published article (Zhan et al., 2022), in which the ASBR was started up 
by gradually increasing OLR, and then the ground WS and PL with a 
weight ratio of 1:1 were loaded to the ASBR with water to reach a 
substrate total solids level (TS, %) of 4 %. The ASBR was operated 
following a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 16 days. Based on the 
properties of PL and WS summarized in Table 1, the daily loading weight 
of PL and WS was found to be 16.72 g for both. The exchange volume of 
the liquid digestate to the loaded substrate was 0.75 L daily to satisfy the 
operation parameters above. The organic loading rate (OLR) was 
calculated to be 1.72 g VS/ (LR⋅d) in this study (LR was the reactor 
working volume in L). 
The two identical ASBRs were operated simultaneously using the 
same substrate loading parameter and monitored for three periods. The 
first period (period 1) was the initial stage before micro-aeration was 
applied, which lasted for 16 days (1 HRT). In the subsequent period of 
16 days, daily micro-aeration was applied, and in the third period of 10 
days, micro-aeration was not employed. For comparison, the first 
reactor (R1) was the blank in which no micro-aeration was applied. 
While daily micro-aeration was applied to the second reactor (R2) in the 
second period (period 2) by injecting air using an air pump (Uniclife Air 
Pump UL40, Uniclife @ Amazon.com) for 0.5 h/day at an air flow rate of 
0.75 L per hour controlled by a flow meter, which was 13.46 N mL air/g 
vS In each period, intermittent mixing was conducted twice daily, each 
for 10 min, and the solid sludge level after each period was controlled at 
4 L. The produced biogas was collected in Tedlar® gas bags (Tedlar Bag, 
CEL Scientific Corp., Cerritos, CA, USA) through the top outlet (Fig. 1), 
and the gas bag was replaced daily. The collected biogas for each day 
was measured in volume and composition. In the meantime, the daily 
discharged effluent from the discharging outlet (Fig. 1) was sampled 
(125 mL) for physio-chemical analysis of total chemical oxygen demand 
(TCOD, mg/L). The effluent in the last five days of each period when the 
digestion process had entered a steady state was also analyzed for other 
physio-chemical parameters including soluble chemical oxygen demand 
(sCOD, mg/L), total volatile fatty acids (TVFA, mg HAc/L), and total 
alkalinity (ALK, g CaCO3/L). 
2.5. Sample analysis 
2.5.1. Physio-chemical parameters analysis 
Total solids (TS) and total volatile solids (TVS) were analyzed 
following the gravity method (Apha, 1998) using an oven (BINDER Inc., 
Bohemia, NY, USA) setting at 105 ℃ and a muffle furnace (Cole-Parmer, 
Vernon Hills, IL, USA) setting at 550 ℃, respectively. Total chemical 
oxygen demand (TCOD), soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD), total 
volatile fatty acids (TVFA), total alkalinity (ALK) of the liquid samples 
were analyzed following the standard methods (Apha, 1998). All these 
parameters were measured in triplicates and the mean values with 
standard deviations were obtained. 
2.5.2. Biogas analysis 
The biogas volume was measured using a wet gas test meter (Model 
XMF-1, Shanghai Cixi Instrument Co., ltd, China). The biogas volume 
was normalized using a gas factor of 0.92 calculated by (Olojede et al., 
2018). The collected gas in gas bags was sampled and the composition 
was analyzed using a Shimadzu Gas Chromatograph (GC 2014, Shi­
madzu Scientific Instruments, Inc., Maryland, CO, USA) equipped with a 
thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a ShinCarbon column (Restek, 
length 2 m × ID 2 mm). The operation of GC was described by Shen and 
Zhu (2017). The percentage of each gas composition could be obtained 
from the percentage value of peak area, with a peak corresponding to a 
specific gas. 
2.6. Data analysis 
The data in this study were recorded, processed, and graphed using 
Excel 2016 (Microsoft, WA, USA). The kinetic model was fitted using the 
solver tool in Excel 2016. Statistical significance was determined by 
analysis of variance (ANOVA) using JMP software (JMP Pro Version 
12.0, SAS Institute Inc., NC, USA) with a p-value of 0.05. Tukey’s Honest 
Significant Difference (HSD) test was used to compare differences of the 
performance of the two ASBRs in different periods.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of different micro-aeration strategies on mono-digestion of 
straw 
The volumetric variation of daily methane production (DMP, N mL), 
the methane content (MC, %) in the produced biogas, and the cumulated 
methane yield (CMY, N mL CH4/g vS added) during batch operation of the 
anaerobic mono-digestion (Mo-AD) of straw are summarized and shown 
in Fig. 2 (a), (b), and (c), respectively. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), pMA, pMA 
+ sMA, and dMA all improved the maximum DMP with reduced lag 
times. Compared with the control (C), which had the maximum DMP 
(123.64 N mL) on day 8, pMA and pMA + sMA arrived at the maximum 
DMP (143.23, and 135.24 N mL, respectively) on day 6, while dMA 
reduced the time to reach the maximum DMP (125.20 N mL) on day 7. 
The results indicated that micro-aeration at the initial stage (pMA or 
dMA) of straw digestion could improve the methane production effi­
ciency by increasing the maximum methane yield as well as reducing the 
time to reach the maximums. In addition, both sMA and pMA + sMA 
showed obvious increase of DMP (94.8 % and 67.0 %, respectively) on 
day 20 (Fig. 2 (a)) after the secondary micro-aeration, indicating that 
micro-aeration during the middle stage of Mo-AD could further improve 
the methane production efficiency. Data of dMA showed a higher DMP 
than that of C during the operation, implying that daily micro-aeration 
could continuously improve methane production, which was consistent 
with the conclusion of Fu et al. (2016) that batch AD of corn straw with 
daily micro-aeration had better daily methane yield than the batch AD 
without micro-aeration. 
Micro-aeration could also affect the methane content (MC) in the 
produced biogas. As shown in Fig. 2 (b), the MC in pMA and pMA + sMA 
was obviously lower than that in C in the first 5 days when micro- 
aeration was applied. In addition, sMA and pMA + sMA also showed 
lower MC than that of C on day 20 and 21 when micro-aeration was 
applied during the middle stage (from day 19 to day 20). However, the 
MC was soon recovered to a similar level of C after micro-aeration was 
stopped. The results implied that micro-aeration in either the pretreat­
ment stage or the middle stage could temporarily decrease the MC in the 
biogas. The observation that the MC of dMA dropped sharply after day 
30 was largely caused by the decrease of methane production activity in 
combination of the injection of air to the digester, which contained a 
large percentage of nitrogen gas that could not be used, leading to a 
rapid decrease of MC in the collected biogas. 
Lastly, as shown in Fig. 2 (c), the CMY were 181.44, 191.01, 187.24, 
200.25, and 211.29 N mL CH4/g vS added for C, pMA, sMA, pMA + sMA, 
and dMA, respectively. All the groups with micro-aeration had relatively 
higher CMY than C, indicating that all the micro-aeration strategies 
enhanced the CMY of Mo-AD of WS. This was consistent with the find­
ings from previous studies that reported enhanced methane yield of AD 
process with micro-aeration applied in different stages (Amin et al., 
2021; Fu et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2015). All the micro-aeration strategies 
improved methane production performance. In this study, the highest 
CMY was obtained in dMA, with an increase of 16.5 % compared with 
that of C. The results pointed out that, among the four micro-aeration 
strategies investigated in this study, daily micro-aeration was the most 
efficient one in improving methane yield in Mo-AD of WS. However, the 
observed CMY of Mo-AD with dMA was still relatively low as opposed to 
the findings in many other studies (Li et al., 2015). Nonetheless, 
improvement in methane yield could be achieved by Co-AD process of 
WS with PL based on the results from previous research (Li et al., 2020; 
Paranhos et al., 2020). Therefore, Co-AD of WS with PL under micro- 
aeration was further investigated. 
3.2. Effect of micro-aeration on co-digestion of wheat straw with poultry 
litter 
The variations of DMP (N mL CH4), MC (%), and the CMY (N mL 
CH4/g vS added) of anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of WS with PL using 
two groups of batch reactors were shown in Fig. 3 (a), (b), and (c), 
respectively, including the control group (Co-C), and the group with 
daily micro-aeration employed (Co-MA). First, the Co-AD process 
improved the methane production efficiency from the Mo-AD. The CMY 
of Co-C (195.84 N mL CH4/g vS added) was 7.9 % higher than that of C 
(181.44 N mL CH4/g vS added). The Co-AD group with micro-aeration 
(Co-MA) also showed an increased CMY (6.7 %) as opposed to the Mo- 
AD group with the same micro-aeration strategy (dMA). The results 
indicated that Co-AD of WS with PL had a better methane production 
efficiency than Mo-AD of WS. This observation was consistent with the 
results from many previous studies that methane production could be 
enhanced by co-digestion of agricultural wastes with animal waste 
(Karki et al., 2021; Paranhos et al., 2020). 
Besides, similar to the findings in the Mo-AD process, micro-aeration 
also improved methane production for the Co-AD process. Compared to 
Co-C, the Co-MA had a slightly higher maximum DMP (158.01 N mL vs 
151.83 N mL) but a shorter digestion time (6 days vs 7 days) to reach the 
maximum. Furthermore, the CMY of Co-MA (225.44 N mL CH4/g vS 
added) was improved by 15.1 % (see Supplementary materialsl), indi­
cating an enhanced methane production efficiency of Co-AD by daily 
micro-aeration, as it was seen in Mo-AD. As a result, the Co-AD of WS

3.3. Kinetic analysis 
3.3.1. Model evaluation 
Five models including the first-order kinetic model, the modified 
Gompertz model, the Cone model, the transfer model and the Chen and 
Hashimoto model were used to fit the measured data of batch MO-AD 
and Co-AD experiments. The calculated parameters for evaluation of 
the fitted models are summarized in Table 3. In general, all five models 
showed good fitting with R2 ˃ 0.9590. However, the modified Gompertz 
model and the Cone model had better goodness-of-fit than the other 
three models according to the comparisons of model evaluation pa­
rameters as shown in Table 3 and the comparisons of model fitting 
curves (see Supplementary materials). Previous studies also identified 
that the first-order kinetic model (Xu et al., 2021; Zhen et al., 2021) or 
the modified Gompertz model (Amin et al., 2021; Zhen et al., 2021) 
could be used to simulate the methane production kinetics of AD process 
under micro-aeration. 
The R2 values of the first-order kinetic model (ranging from 0.9590 
to 0.9774), the Chen and Hashimoto model (ranging from 0.9722 to 
0.9842) were obviously lower than those of the transfer model (ranging 
from 0.9856 to 0.9939) and were even lower than those of the modified 
Gompertz model (ranging from 0.9979 to 0.9997) and the Cone model 
(ranging from 0.9979 to 0.9996). The Cone model had slightly higher R2 
values (0.9994, 0.9996) than the modified Gompertz model (0.9980, 
0.9987) in the Co-AD experiments, indicating that the Cone model fitted 
slightly better in methane yield of the Co-AD process. This observation 
was consistent with the reports from previous studies (El-Mashad, 2013; 
Li et al., 2015). Also, the modified Gompertz model and the Cone model 
had lower rMSPE values (ranging from 1.03 to 3.17 and from 1.48 to 
2.64, respectively) than the first-order kinetic model (ranging from 9.16 
to 13.06), the Chen and Hashimoto model (ranging from 7.64 to 10.25), 
and the transfer model (ranging from 4.75 to 6.95), suggesting a good 
correlation between the predicted and the measured values by the two 
models. The lower values of AIC and BIC of the modified Gompertz 
model (from 11.66 to 89.99, and from 13.00 to 91.33, respectively) and 
the Cone model (from 36.56 to 77.28, and from 37.89 to 78.61, 
respectively) demonstrated that they were more suitable for fitting the 
experimental data than the first-order kinetic model (both larger than 
160), the Chen and Hashimoto model (both larger than 150), and the 
transfer model (both larger than 120). Finally, the overall Difference (%) 
was the smallest for the modified Gompertz model (-0.13 to 1.08), fol­
lowed by the Cone model (4.39 to 9.37), the transfer model (4.53 to 
10.02), the first-order kinetic model (10.23 to 19.33) and the Chen and 
Hashimoto model (35.57 to 51.46). The variation curves of the five 
models (see Supplementary materials) again illustrated that the modi­
fied Gompertz and Cone models correlated with the measured data 
much better than the first-order kinetic model, the transfer model, and 
the Chen and Hashimoto model. Therefore, these two models could be 
considered more suitable than the other three models in simulating the 
methane yield kinetics of micro-aeration assisted Mo-AD and Co-AD 
processes due to the relatively higher R2 and lower rMSPE, AIC, BIC, 
and Difference (%). And the Cone model was slightly better for the Co- 
AD process than the modified Gompertz model. 
3.3.2. Kinetic constants 
The obtained kinetic constants from the three models such as the 
maximum methane yield potential (Ym), maximum methane yield rate 
(Rm), hydrolysis rate constant (k), lag phase duration (λ), the shape 
factor (n), the Chen and Hashimoto constant (kCH) and the maximum 
specific growth rate of microorganisms (μm) in different experiments 
were summarized, compared, and used to assess the effect of micro- 
aeration on the kinetic performance of AD processes (Table 3). 
The maximum methane yield (Ym) is a predictor of methane pro­
duction potential based on substrate usage (Shamurad et al., 2020). It 
could be observed from Table 3 that the variation trend of Ym for all 
models were consistent with the variation of measured CMY in both Mo- 
AD and Co-AD experiments, and Ym was improved by different micro- 
aeration methods to varying degrees as discussed in Section 3.1 and 
3.2, respectively. The predicted Ym by the modified Gompertz model 
with a lower value of Difference (%) was closer to the measured CMY

The hydrolysis rate constant (k), a parameter used to characterize the 
degradation rate of the substrate, can be calculated for the first-order 
kinetic model and the Cone model. A larger k value meant a higher 
degradation rate (Zhen et al., 2015). In general, the k value obtained 
from the Cone model (ranging from 0.102 to 0.142 d-1) was slightly 
higher than that from the first-order model (from 0.063 to 0.100 d-1). 
Considering the same variation of the k value between the two models 
and that the Cone model fitted better than the first-order kinetic model, 
different groups was compared with reference to the k value of the Cone 
model. For the Mo-AD group, pMA had the largest k value (0.129 d-1), 
followed by pMA + sMA (0.116 d-1), and they both were larger than the 
k value of C (0.115 d-1). However, sMA and dMA both showed a lower k 
value (0.106 and 0.103 d-1, respectively) than C. These results indicated 
that different micro-aeration strategies produced different impacts on 
the hydrolysis rate constant (k), i.e., pretreatment micro-aeration could 
enhance the hydrolysis rate, but secondary micro-aeration and daily 
micro-aeration had a negative effect on the k value. Despite that, they all 
improved the methane yield (Ym) compared to C. The improvement of 
methane production due to pretreatment micro-aeration could be 
attributed to enhanced hydrolysis, but the reason for the improvement 
of methane production associated with the secondary micro-aeration 
was not straightforward, and could result from other pathways such as 
digestion of refractory organic matters, scavenging hydrogen sulfide by 
methanogens (Krayzelova et al., 2015) to maintain VFAs conversion (Fu 
et al., 2015). And daily micro-aeration could improve methane pro­
duction by maintaining low VFAs concentration, or by promoting mi­
crobial activities (Fu et al., 2016) due to the small but continuous dosage 
of oxygen. For the Co-AD, the k value of Co-C (0.124 d-1) and Co-MA 
(0.112 d-1) were larger than that of C and dMA in the Mo-AD group, 
indicating that co-digestion improved substrate hydrolysis. Karki et al. 
(2021) concluded that co-digestion process could achieve enhanced 
digestibility due to synergistic effects of co-substrates and better process 
stability compared to the mono-digestion process. In addition, daily 
micro-aeration again showed a negative effect on k value, which was 
lower in Co-MA than in Co-C. 
The constants of Rm, the maximum methane yield rate (N mL CH4/g 
vS added /d), and λ, the lag phase duration (d), both obtained from the 
modified Gompertz model or the transfer model, were important pa­
rameters to evaluate the AD process. A higher value of Rm and a shorter 
value of λ indicated a higher maximum methane production activity.

3.4. Performance of the continuous co-digestion of wheat straw and 
poultry litter with micro-aeration 
Although the methane yield was generally higher in batch operation 
mode of AD reactors, the continuous-flow mode was normally employed 
in AD plants for undisrupted energy production (Zahan et al., 2018a). 
Thus, the performance of micro-aeration assisted Co-AD of WS and PL in 
continuous-flow mode was further investigated using ASBR based on the 
results of the batch experiments. The effect of daily micro-aeration on 
the ASBR performance was examined by monitoring and comparing the 
two reactors in different running periods. The daily variation of the 
biogas production rate (BPR, L/(LR⋅d)) and the biogas composition 
(including contents (%) of methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), and 
nitrogen (N2)) for R1 and R2 were shown in Fig. 4 (a) and (b), respec­
tively. The comparison of the daily methane yield (DMY, N mL CH4/g vS 
added) and the total chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) variation between 
R1 and R2 were shown in Fig. 4 (c). And the performance of the two 
reactors in the steady state of each period were compared and summa­
rized in Table 4. 
For the blank reactor R1, the variation was basically stable in the 
three periods as shown in Fig. 4 (a) and (c). The average values of BPR, 
methane (CH4) content, CH4/CO2 ratio (v/v) and DMY were (0.38 ±
0.01) N L/(LR⋅d), (52.78 ± 0.51) %, 1.16 ± 0.02, and (117.23 ± 4.32) N 
mL CH4/g vS added, respectively. And the effluent analysis also showed 
relatively stable readings of TCOD (Fig. 4 (c)). The average content of 
TCOD, soluble COD (sCOD), total volatile fatty acids (TVFA), and total 
alkalinity (ALK) in the effluent were (1597.62 ± 31.61) mg /L, (727.78 
± 26.47) mg /L, (272.11 ± 6.45) mg HAc/L and (1.24 ± 0.04) g CaCO3/ 
L, respectively. 
For R2, in general, the ASBR had a significantly higher BPR in period 
2 when micro-aeration was applied but a slightly lower CH4 content in 
the produced biogas (Fig. 4 (b)), resulting in a significantly higher DMY 
compared to that in period 1 and period 3 (Fig. 4 (c)). In period 1, the 
relatively stable performance of the continuous ASBR was similar to that 
of R1 (no significant difference, p greater than 0.05), showing a BPR of 
(0.38 ± 0.01) N L/(LR⋅d), a CH4 content of (52.85 ± 0.27) %, and a DMY 
of (115.89 ± 4.02) N mL CH4/g vS added. After micro-aeration was 
applied in period 2, the methane production performance was signifi­
cantly enhanced (p < 0.05). The BPR ((0.48 ± 0.01) N L/(LR⋅d)) was 
increased by 26.9 % and DMY ((140.75 ± 2.82) N mL CH4/g vS added was 
increased by 21.5 %, while the CH4 content slightly decreased to (50.60 
± 0.11) %. The methane production of R2 with micro-aeration in period 
2 was also significantly higher than that of R1 in the same period. The 
DMY of R2 was significantly higher (18.34 %) than that of R1 in period 2 
(Fig. 4 (c)). Moreover, when micro-aeration was stopped in period 3, the 
methane production efficiency showed a significant decline compared to 
in period 2. The BPR dropped to (0.41 ± 0.01) N L/(LR⋅d) and the DMY 
decreased to (128.05 ± 2.20) N mL CH4/g vS added, but, interestingly, 
the CH4 content was recovered to (54.10 ± 0.17) %. The results indi­
cated that daily micro-aeration significantly enhanced methane pro­
duction performance in the continuous-flow ASBR for co-digestion of 
WS and PL. The observation of enhanced methane production perfor­
mance by micro-aeration was consistent with the findings from previous 
studies that applied micro-aeration to the continuous-flow AD process in 
other reactor configurations. For instance, Zhu et al. (2022) employed 
micro-aeration in a semi-continued AD reactor under different organic 
loading rates (OLRs) and reported that micro-aeration increased the 
median daily methane yields by 6 %, 10 %, and 8 % at OLRs of 1.1, 1.5, 
and 2.1 g VS/(L⋅day), respectively. D. Nguyen et al. (2019a) adopted 
intermittent (every 24 h), ORP-controlled micro-aeration for the AD of 
lignocellulosic biomass in a continuous-stirred tank reactor (CSTR) and 
found that a stable digester performance was obtained with an improved 
methane yield due to the rapid VFA conversion and methane production

4. Conclusions 
Daily micro-aeration could increase the CMY most in Mo-AD of WS 
by 16.5 %. The CMY was 15.1 % improved (225.44 N mL CH4/g vS added) 
from the Co-AD of WS and PL with micro-aeration. The modified 
Gompertz model and Cone model were able to accurately fit the 
methane yield kinetics data of the micro-aeration assisted AD process 
(R2 greater than 0.99). With micro-aeration, the ASBR for continuous 
Co-AD of WS and PL achieved an enhanced performance with an in­
crease in DMY by 21.5 %. The results indicated that micro-aeration in 
AD of agricultural wastes could be an appropriate technology for real 
applications.
